text: Ana’s train crossed the plains through sixteen hours of rain, stopping at stations with shuttered kiosks and dripping platform roofs. She had paid extra for a sleeper after working three overnight shifts. At midnight, a conductor examined her ticket and ordered her into the corridor. Her compartment, he said, was needed for someone traveling on a premium account. Ana held out the reservation again. He pushed her hand aside and unlocked the door for a man carrying polished leather bags. “Take it up at the terminal.” The latch clicked behind him. Heat climbed Ana’s neck. Her fingers tightened around the ticket until its edges cut into her palm. They had taken her money, then handed her bed to someone worth more to them. She planted her suitcase across the corridor and demanded the conductor’s employee number. When he tried to step around it, she dragged it back into his path. She would not make this convenient for him.
first_sentence: Ana’s train crossed the plains through sixteen hours of rain, stopping at stations with shuttered kiosks and dripping platform roofs.

text: Lukas boarded the overnight train with a canvas bag, a reserved sleeper ticket, and sixteen hours of track ahead. By midnight, he had spent six hours upright beside the rattling carriage door because the conductor had given his berth to another passenger. Each time Lukas presented his ticket, the conductor tapped a clipboard and walked away. Then Lukas saw the passenger slip folded banknotes into the conductor’s pocket. His jaw locked. Heat climbed his neck beneath his collar, and he gripped the ticket until its stiff edges cut his palm. He followed the conductor into the corridor and planted himself across the narrow passage. “Check it again.” The conductor reached past him for the door handle. Lukas struck the wall with his open hand, hard enough to silence the nearby conversation. He had paid for that bed. He would not spend another mile making room for the man who had sold it twice.
first_sentence: Lukas boarded the overnight train with a canvas bag, a reserved sleeper ticket, and sixteen hours of track ahead.

text: Leila’s train crossed the salt plains through the afternoon, twelve hours into a journey that would last until morning. She had paid extra for a sleeper after three weeks of double shifts, and kept the reservation folded inside her ticket. At dusk, a conductor knocked and ordered her into the corridor. A passenger in a tailored coat stood behind him, carrying no bedding. “He needs this compartment,” the conductor said. Leila showed her reservation. He glanced at it, then dropped it onto her suitcase and opened the door wider for the other passenger. Heat climbed her neck. Her jaw tightened until a tooth ached. So her money counted when they took it, but her place counted only until someone better dressed wanted it. She planted her suitcase across the doorway. When the conductor reached for its handle, she slapped her palm over his and held his gaze. Behind her, the neatly made berth remained empty.
first_sentence: Leila’s train crossed the salt plains through the afternoon, twelve hours into a journey that would last until morning.

text: Bruno played midfield on a municipal pitch where crooked nets hung between rusted posts and substitutes sat on kit bags. With five minutes left, he intercepted a pass and drove toward the penalty area. A defender hooked both arms around his waist and dragged him down. The referee waved play on. Bruno sprang up, grass stuck to his cheek, and pointed at the torn seam of his shirt. “You were looking straight at him.” The referee showed him a yellow card while the defender covered a grin with his hand. Heat climbed Bruno’s neck. His jaw locked so tightly that his back teeth ached. Apparently, getting hauled down counted for nothing; objecting was the offense. He crushed a fistful of his shirt, then released it before the fabric split further. When play restarted, he sprinted after the ball, each breath scraping his throat, unable to stop replaying that hidden grin.
first_sentence: Bruno played midfield on a municipal pitch where crooked nets hung between rusted posts and substitutes sat on kit bags.

text: Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch beside the railway tracks. With ten minutes left, he intercepted a pass and broke toward the penalty area. So that was how the afternoon worked: one shirt bought a whistle, the other bought a mouthful of earth. He marched toward the referee, fists clamped against his shorts. “You watched him do it.” The referee reached for a card without answering. Hiroshi's jaw locked. He kicked a loose clod so hard it burst across the white line, then stood breathing through his nose.
first_sentence: Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch beside the railway tracks.

text: At two in the morning, Fatima stood beside a conveyor belt beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. The supervisor crossed out two hours and initialed the change. “You took too long,” he said. Behind him, his nephew’s untouched sheet already bore approval for a full shift. Heat climbed Fatima’s neck. She pressed her tongue against her teeth until her jaw ached. Those missing hours were groceries, bus fare, the money she had stretched all week. He slid the sheet back as though she had handed him rubbish. Her fingers closed around the pen hard enough to blanch. She wanted to sweep his neat little desk onto the floor. Instead, she photographed both sheets, then demanded the correction, keeping her palm flat over her own.
first_sentence: At two in the morning, Fatima stood beside a conveyor belt beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights.

text: At midnight, Malik worked beneath the strip lights of a warehouse, stacking cartons beside a loading bay. text: Chloe stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a display of quilts and handwritten household records. She would not move aside. Let their guests watch them try to erase her twice.
first_sentence: Chloe stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a display of quilts and handwritten household records.

text: Mira stood beneath the museum’s glass dome with a special exhibition ticket folded inside her guidebook. At the gallery entrance, an attendant scanned it, then blocked the doorway with his arm. first_sentence: Mira stood beneath the museum’s glass dome with a special exhibition ticket folded inside her guidebook.

text: Andrei stood beneath the museum’s glass dome beside a display of bronze vessels. He snatched the book back, his fingers shaking against its leather cover. “You tore it.” The guard shrugged and pointed toward the exit. text: At seven fifteen, Ibrahim stood beside the bus shelter as rain streaked the timetable glass. When the bus arrived, he joined the queue with his pass ready. The reader flashed green, but the driver thrust an arm across the aisle. “Pay again.” Ibrahim pointed to the screen and the deduction on his phone. The driver looked past both and waved the next passenger through without checking her ticket. Behind him, someone told him to stop holding everyone up. Heat climbed his neck. He pressed his teeth together until his jaw ached, staring at the green light that had already proved him right. His shift began in twenty minutes; another delay meant another warning. He dropped coins into the machine, each one striking metal harder than necessary. Walking down the aisle, he gripped the receipt so tightly its edge cut his thumb. He pictured laying both charges on the depot counter and refusing to leave.
first_sentence: At seven fifteen, Ibrahim stood beside the bus shelter as rain streaked the timetable glass.

text: Ana boarded the train at six and placed a notebook beside the window. The route covered 960 kilometers over 12 hours, so she calculated 960 divided by 12 equaled 80 kilometers per hour. Between stations, fields passed behind rows of utility poles. She counted 24 poles in one stretch and 18 in another; 24 plus 18 equaled 42. Each carriage had 16 rows with 4 seats per row, and she wrote that 16 multiplied by 4 equaled 64 seats. After the train covered 375 kilometers, she subtracted 375 from 960 and recorded 585 kilometers remaining. At a station, several passengers exchanged places with others on the platform. Ana measured two sections of the printed route with a ruler: 7 centimeters plus 9 centimeters equaled 16 centimeters. She folded the map along its existing creases. Later, she divided 180 minutes by 60, noted 3 hours, and returned the notebook to her bag.
first_sentence: Ana boarded the train at six and placed a notebook beside the window.

text: Lukas boarded the train at six and placed his notebook beside the window. The journey covered 840 kilometers, and at an average of 70 kilometers per hour, 840 divided by 70 equaled 12 hours. The train continued through several tunnels, and he closed the notebook when the carriage lights came on.

text: Leila boarded the train at dawn and placed a notebook beside the window. The route covered 840 kilometers, and she divided 840 by 70 to calculate 12 hours of travel. text: Carlos traveled north on a train scheduled to cross the region in sixteen hours. He opened a notebook beside the window and recorded the carriage numbers. The first two were 24 and 36; he wrote 24 + 36 = 60 beneath them. At the next station, he counted 48 platform tiles along one section and subtracted the 19 covered by a parked trolley: 48 − 19 = 29. The train continued between fields. Each visible fence panel had 7 upright bars, so he calculated 8 × 7 = 56 for eight panels. After lunch, he divided the route’s 960 kilometers by 16 hours and wrote 960 ÷ 16 = 60 kilometers per hour. He then counted 12 compartments with 6 seats each: 12 × 6 = 72. Outside, fields gave way to warehouses. Carlos turned the page, entered the time, and continued listing distances as the carriage moved along the tracks.
first_sentence: Carlos traveled north on a train scheduled to cross the region in sixteen hours.

text: Beatriz stood beside the amateur football pitch with a notebook and a pencil. Each team had 11 players, so she wrote 11 + 11 = 22 beside the starting formation. The match consisted of two halves of 35 minutes; she calculated 2 × 35 = 70 minutes of play. After 18 minutes, she subtracted 35 − 18 = 17 to record the time remaining in the first half. A substitute walked along the touchline while the ball passed between three defenders. Beatriz counted 24 completed passes across four stretches of play and divided 24 ÷ 4 = 6 passes per stretch. At the interval, she measured the pitch on a printed diagram: 9 centimeters represented 90 meters, giving 90 ÷ 9 = 10 meters per centimeter. During the second half, each side scored once. She entered 1 + 1 = 2 total goals, closed the notebook, and collected the cones after the final whistle.

text: Bruno played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch. Before kickoff, he counted 11 players on each team and calculated that 11 + 11 = 22 players occupied the field. text: Ana’s train crossed the mountain plateau on the second night of its journey, its windows silvered by sleet. She had spent the day counting tunnels and folding the corners of a timetable. Near midnight, a sharp crack rang beneath her carriage. Her cup slid off the table. Then the train gathered speed, although the timetable showed a station just beyond the descending curve. Outside, sparks streamed against the glass. A conductor hurried down the aisle, pulling at a radio that answered only with static. Ana gripped his sleeve; he barely stopped. “Get down between the seats.” She crouched, her knees striking the floor, and tried to swallow through a throat that had closed tight. The wheels shrieked. Ahead, through the connecting doorway, carriage lights swung violently from side to side. She pictured the ravine they had crossed that afternoon and pressed both hands over her head, waiting for the floor to vanish.
first_sentence: Ana’s train crossed the mountain plateau on the second night of its journey, its windows silvered by sleet.

text: Lukas sat beside a scratched window as the overnight train crossed the mountains on the thirteenth hour of its journey. Empty cups rattled on his table, and the dark glass reflected rows of sleeping passengers. Then the brakes caught hard enough to throw his bag into the aisle. The train stopped inside a tunnel. For several seconds, nothing moved except a newspaper sliding from someone’s lap. A dull impact sounded overhead. Water began pouring through a seam above the carriage door. Lukas pulled his feet onto the seat as a black stream spread across the floor. He pressed the emergency intercom, but its button stayed dark. Farther down the carriage, someone tugged uselessly at a door handle. His tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. He pictured the miles of mountain above them, the tunnel filling from both ends. When the lights went out, he gripped the seat until his fingernails bent.
first_sentence: Lukas sat beside a scratched window as the overnight train crossed the mountains on the thirteenth hour of its journey.

text: Leila’s train had crossed three provinces by midnight and was climbing through the mountains beneath a sky without stars. She folded her coat against the window and counted the remaining hours until morning. Beyond the glass, scattered lights disappeared as the track entered a tunnel. Then a sharp crack whipped through the carriage, followed by a grinding noise beneath her feet. Her cup slid off the table. The train gathered speed. Across the aisle, a sleeping passenger lurched forward, and the ceiling lights flickered out. Leila gripped the armrests so tightly that her nails bent. Somewhere ahead lay the viaduct she had seen on the route map, a thin line stretched over a gorge. The grinding stopped, but the rushing wheels only grew louder. She reached for the emergency handle with a shaking hand. It hung loose when she pulled it. In the darkness, she braced her feet against the seat opposite and waited for the tunnel to end.
first_sentence: Leila’s train had crossed three provinces by midnight and was climbing through the mountains beneath a sky without stars.

text: On Sunday afternoon, Bruno played goalkeeper in an amateur football match on a pitch behind the railway depot. The teams had marked the touchlines with flour and dragged two old metal goals out of a shed. During the second half, a shot struck the crossbar above him. The frame shifted with a dry scrape. Bruno glanced down and saw one rear support lift clear of the ground. Beyond the post, a small child sat tying a shoelace. Another shot was already coming. Bruno's mouth went dry; his pulse hammered so hard that he barely heard the players calling. If the ball hit the bar again, the whole frame could fall forward. He tried to shout, but only a thin rasp came out. Abandoning the ball, he lunged around the post and pulled the child sideways. Metal crashed against the turf behind them. Bruno stayed crouched, gripping the child's sleeve, unable to make his fingers open.
first_sentence: On Sunday afternoon, Bruno played goalkeeper in an amateur football match on a pitch behind the railway depot.

text: Hiroshi played right back in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch beside the railway. The teams had marked the touchlines with flour, and someone had weighted the portable goals with sandbags. Late in the second half, a cross sailed over him. Even after the child stood clear, Hiroshi kept pulling, his fingers locked around the cloth.

text: At two in the morning, Fatima scanned cartons beneath the warehouse strip lights while rain tapped the loading bays. There was nowhere beneath those pallets that her body could fit and survive. She dropped flat and crawled toward the narrow gap under the gate, dragging one boot behind her as another bolt fell.

text: The train carried Ana across three provinces, past harvested fields and stations lit by single yellow lamps. text: Lukas had spent eighteen hours on the train as it crossed wheat fields, river bridges, and a range of low mountains. text: Agnes began her night shift at the warehouse by hanging her burgundy coat beside a row of red lockers. text: Chloe entered the museum through a vermilion doorway and placed her red umbrella in a cylindrical stand. Beneath a crimson ceiling, she collected a floor plan printed with burgundy borders. In the next room, Chloe read a label describing the pigments used in an old tapestry of red leaves and rust-colored branches. She stopped at a table where visitors could compare samples of madder-dyed wool against maroon cards. An unnamed attendant replaced a red pencil beside the register. Chloe marked the final gallery on her map, returned through the vermilion doorway, and removed her umbrella from the stand. Outside, she followed the red paving stones toward the street.

text: Kenji entered the museum through a vermilion doorway and placed his red umbrella in a cylindrical stand. At the ticket desk, he received a crimson paper pass printed with the floor plan. text: Mira entered the museum through a vermilion doorway and placed her red umbrella in a cylindrical stand. text: Andrei entered the museum through a red wooden door and placed his umbrella beside a crimson bench. At the counter, an attendant handed him a ticket printed on scarlet paper. text: Ingrid reached the bus stop at seven, carrying a red canvas bag beneath her burgundy coat. The timetable sat inside a crimson frame, beside an advertisement showing tomatoes in a scarlet bowl. Ingrid placed her bag on her knees and held a ticket printed with a thin red border. Across the aisle, a passenger folded a newspaper over a vermilion lunch container. The bus passed brick warehouses, red awnings, and a bicycle with cherry-colored wheel rims. At the next stop, two passengers boarded with matching russet shopping bags. first_sentence: Ingrid reached the bus stop at seven, carrying a red canvas bag beneath her burgundy coat.

text: Viktor reached the bus stop beside a red brick wall, carrying a burgundy canvas bag. The timetable sat beneath a crimson header, and a red advertisement covered one side of the shelter. text: Ana’s train crossed the plains beneath a low October sky, its windows streaked with rain. She had packed two oranges, a clean blouse, and the book her father had asked her to read aloud when she arrived. For seventeen hours, she watched stations slide past and measured the remaining distance with her thumb on a folded timetable. Beyond the mountains, her phone rang. A nurse told her that her father had died six minutes earlier. Ana kept the phone against her ear after the call ended. The carriage rocked; someone unwrapped a sandwich. She opened the book and found the scrap of paper marking their place halfway through a chapter. Her throat closed around a breath. She pressed the paper flat against her knee, then folded over it until her forehead touched the seat ahead. Outside, the tracks continued toward the room where nobody would ask her to turn another page.
first_sentence: Ana’s train crossed the plains beneath a low October sky, its windows streaked with rain.

text: Lukas sat beside the window of a northbound train, with a canvas bag beneath his knees and twelve hours of track ahead. Inside the bag lay a blue cardigan he had bought for his mother, its sleeves folded around a tin of biscuits. At each station, he checked the time and counted the stops remaining. Beyond the glass, harvested fields gave way to factories, then fields again. His phone rang while the conductor was punching tickets. He listened, pressing one finger against his other ear. “When?” he asked. The conductor moved on. Lukas kept the phone against his cheek after the call ended. Then he pulled out the cardigan and unfolded it across his lap. He had chosen the larger buttons because her fingers had grown stiff. His mouth opened, but his breath would not come properly. For the remaining six hours, he held one sleeve between both hands while the train carried him toward her empty room.
first_sentence: Lukas sat beside the window of a northbound train, with a canvas bag beneath his knees and twelve hours of track ahead.

text: The overnight train carried Leila north through wheat fields, freight yards, and towns with a single light above each platform. She had packed two oranges and the cardigan her father always said was too thin. At every stop, she checked the remaining distance and rehearsed how she would walk into his hospital room without mentioning the years between visits. Near dawn, her phone vibrated. A nurse spoke for less than a minute. Leila kept the phone against her ear after the call ended, listening to the wheels beneath the carriage. Then she took out an orange and pressed her thumb into its skin until juice ran down her wrist. There would be no room to enter, no opportunity to let him interrupt her apology. Across the aisle, a passenger offered a tissue. She folded it into smaller and smaller squares while the train continued north, carrying her toward a station where nobody would be waiting.
first_sentence: The overnight train carried Leila north through wheat fields, freight yards, and towns with a single light above each platform.

text: Bruno played left back on a muddy municipal pitch between a railway embankment and a row of garages. His father’s old scarf hung from the fence beside the substitutes, its wool darkened by drizzle. At halftime, while the others passed around orange slices, a woman from the hospital called his phone. His father had died twenty minutes earlier. Bruno kept pressing the phone against his ear after she had finished, listening to the empty connection. That morning, his father had told him to play; there would be other afternoons for visiting. Across the pitch, someone rolled the ball toward him. It bumped his boot and stopped. He bent to retie a lace that was already knotted, but his fingers would not close around it. When the whistle summoned the teams, he sat beneath the fence instead. He pulled the scarf into his lap and searched its wet folds for the smell of his father’s coat.
first_sentence: Bruno played left back on a muddy municipal pitch between a railway embankment and a row of garages.

text: On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on the council pitch beside the railway. His father sat near the halfway line with a flask between his shoes, as he had every weekend for twenty years. Just before halftime, Hiroshi glanced across to see whether he had watched a pass. The folding chair lay sideways. Two spectators knelt beside it. Hiroshi ran beyond the touchline, still calling for the referee to stop play. Someone pulled him back while another pair of hands pressed against his father's chest. Later, at the hospital, a doctor spoke, and Hiroshi kept staring at the mud drying on his socks. He had left the flask beneath the chair. His father would need it for the trip home. The thought repeated until he understood there would be no trip home together. He bent over his boots and tried to undo a lace, but his fingers could not hold it.
first_sentence: On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on the council pitch beside the railway.

text: At two in the morning, Fatima stood beneath the warehouse strip lights, feeding cartons onto a conveyor belt. Her phone vibrated against her hip, once, then again. She pulled off a glove with her teeth and answered. The nurse said her mother had stopped breathing before they could move her to another room. Fatima watched a box pass with one flap sticking up. She reached to flatten it, missed, and reached again after it had gone. On her phone, beneath the ended call, was the reminder she had set: bring slippers tomorrow. She pressed her thumb against those words until the screen offered to delete them. Then she put the phone away. In the break room, she opened the lunch her mother had packed that afternoon. Two oranges sat beside the rice, peeled in a single curling strip. Fatima folded over the lid, bent across the table, and sobbed into her sleeve until it clung wetly to her mouth.

text: At midnight, Malik moved pallets beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights while rain tapped the loading doors. He had packed two sandwiches, one for his break and one for the hospital afterward. His father had complained about the food there, which Malik took as a reason to keep bringing lunch. At two, his phone vibrated against the forklift’s dashboard. A nurse asked him to sit down. He stayed standing until she finished, then lowered himself onto a wooden pallet. Across the aisle, a conveyor carried cartons toward the trucks. He watched each one disappear through the rubber curtains, unable to remember where he was meant to take his load. When his supervisor approached, Malik held up one finger, still waiting for the nurse to say something else. Later, he opened his lunch bag. He touched the second sandwich through its paper wrapper and bent forward, pressing it against his chest.

topic: a night shift at a warehouse
text: At midnight, Agnes worked beneath the warehouse strip lights, scanning cartons beside the loading bays. When a pallet struck the table, the phone slid beneath a reversing forklift. She raised one hand, too late. The driver stopped and helped her collect the pieces, setting them in a shallow cardboard tray. Agnes pressed the broken power button until its jagged edge marked her thumb. She tried to recall exactly how her mother had pronounced slippers, but the voice in her head had already become her own. Behind her, cartons continued down the conveyor. She folded a packing slip over the shattered screen and sat on the concrete, holding the tray level in both hands.
first_sentence: At midnight, Agnes worked beneath the warehouse strip lights, scanning cartons beside the loading bays.

text: At midnight, Dmitri drove a pallet jack between the warehouse loading bays and the rows of shrink-wrapped crates. Near three, his supervisor handed him a cardboard box from the locker room. They needed the locker for a new hire; his father’s things had stayed there long enough. Dmitri set the box beside the time clock. Inside lay a thermos, a spare pair of socks, and the reading glasses he had searched for after the funeral. One lens still bore a thumbprint. He lifted the thermos and unscrewed its lid. The faint smell of coffee remained beneath the metal smell, and his knees bent until he was sitting on an empty pallet. For thirty years, his father had brought that flask to work. Dmitri pressed the lid against his mouth. When the loading bell rang, he tried to stand, but stayed seated, holding the box steady while his chest hitched and the glasses blurred.
first_sentence: At midnight, Dmitri drove a pallet jack between the warehouse loading bays and the rows of shrink-wrapped crates.

text: Chloe walked through the museum’s textile gallery on a Tuesday afternoon, past glass cases of samplers and wedding lace. She had come to see the quilt her mother had donated years before, when climbing stairs was still possible. At the reception desk, an attendant checked a ledger, then led her to a narrow display near the lifts. Only a square remained. Water from a burst pipe had destroyed the rest, the attendant explained; this section had been salvaged. Chloe placed her palm against the glass. The surviving patch was plain blue, without the crooked yellow bird her mother had sewn for her. She searched its edges anyway, bending until her breath clouded the case. There had been so many chances to photograph that bird. Her knees loosened, and she sat on the floor beside the display, holding her empty hands together as visitors stepped around her.
first_sentence: Chloe walked through the museum’s textile gallery on a Tuesday afternoon, past glass cases of samplers and wedding lace.

text: Mira stood in the museum’s textile gallery beneath a row of narrow skylights. She had come to see the blue coat her mother had stitched from scraps during the year their roof collapsed. Behind glass, it looked smaller than it had on the kitchen table. Mira leaned toward the label, expecting the name she had written carefully on every donation form. It read: Maker unknown. She checked the neighboring labels, then the number on her receipt. Both numbers matched. Her mother had died in February; now even the coat seemed to belong to nobody. Mira pressed her lips together until they hurt. She remembered those bent fingers pushing a needle through three layers, the little dish that held the thread. A guard offered her a bench. She sat with the receipt flattened against her knee, rubbing one printed digit until the paper thinned and split beneath her thumb.
first_sentence: Mira stood in the museum’s textile gallery beneath a row of narrow skylights.

text: Andrei stood beneath the museum’s glass roof beside a display of household objects recovered from the flooded valley. He had donated his mother’s sewing box years earlier, wrapped in a towel, without opening it. Now it sat beneath a light, its compartments arranged for strangers to inspect. Among the buttons and needles lay a folded paper newly uncovered by the curator. He bent toward the label. It was a list in his mother’s handwriting: trousers to shorten, curtains to finish, blue shirt for Andrei’s birthday. The date was three days before the river took her house. He pressed two fingers against the glass, directly above his name. His throat tightened until swallowing hurt. All these years, he had pictured her waiting for rescue; here she was planning his sleeves. He sat on the bench opposite the case and kept his coat on, unable to leave her work unfinished behind him.
first_sentence: Andrei stood beneath the museum’s glass roof beside a display of household objects recovered from the flooded valley.

text: The morning bus carried Ibrahim past shuttered shops and pavement littered with wet leaves. He held two paper cups between his knees, as he did every Thursday when his mother met him outside the hospital after her overnight shift. At the next stop, his phone vibrated. The caller asked whether he was somewhere he could sit down. He looked at the blue seat beneath him and said nothing. His mother had collapsed beside the lockers; they had worked on her for forty minutes. Ibrahim pressed the phone harder against his ear, waiting for the sentence that would undo the others. The bus jolted, spilling coffee over his fingers. He watched it run into his cuff without moving. Outside the hospital, a woman in uniform stood beneath their usual tree. For a moment he lifted the second cup. Then she turned, and he lowered it to the empty seat beside him, carefully, so it would not tip.
first_sentence: The morning bus carried Ibrahim past shuttered shops and pavement littered with wet leaves.
